t: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting – Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims

items.n: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting:1
items.e: He who faileth to visit his intimate friend doeth violence to his soul; but he whose dull visit is one heavy wail, will meet with confusion, insult, and shame.
items.h: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting

items.n: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting:2
items.e: Visit but rarely, attachment will grow; from visits too frequent estrangement will spring.

items.n: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting:3
items.e: Let not a mile be the proverbial stile, when thou shouldst visit the sorrowing and sick; let two miles be as nothing, when as peacemaker thou'rt sought, to cause strife and dissension to cease among men.

items.n: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting:4
items.e: Visit not thy friends at all times and all hours, but keep back thy foot from their dwelling; see, how men long for the showers of rain, when for a time they are kept back from the earth!

items.n: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting:5
items.e: When a bore once came to visit a friend, prolonging his stay to an inordinate length, the patient remarked—"If thou hast business to do, then say so, be quick! Let's be done with the thing! Or if it's a debt thou hast come to claim, then speak of the debt. How much do I owe? I'll give it: Take it and go!"

items.n: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting:6
items.e: O dullard, if thou'lt be advised for thy good, pray visit the sick no longer; for worse, worse by far than the sickness itself, are the visits that prove thee a bore.

items.n: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting:7
items.e: A patient was once asked, "What aileth thee?" And he answered forthwith, "My will, that is stubborn and sinful." They said unto him then, "What is the wish that thou wouldst now ask?" And he answered and said, "My sole wish is that Heaven may forgive me my sins." Again they did ask, "Shall we go and fetch the physician?" And he answered and said, "'Twas he who made me ill." They continued and spake, "Shall we give you some relish?" And his answer was then, "I am sick of all food."

items.n: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting:8
items.e: To keep off the bore from thy circle of friends, have little to do with him, give him no ear.

items.n: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting:9
items.e: Like tasting of honeycomb's droppings, is the pleasure of dining with friends; to dine with men that are hateful to thee, is as bad as the fever and scab.

items.n: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting:10
items.e: When thou seest two in close converse, quickly withdraw and hold back; obtrude not thyself on their presence.

items.n: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting:11
items.e: The world grows sick of the society of those who never cease to prate.

items.n: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting:12
items.e: A King, to get rid of the bore he did hate, bethought him of this fine device: He bade them inscribe on the signet he wore these words which bluntly told him his mind—"Canst thou not see thou art a great bore? O dull one, rise and begone!" And this ring he would turn again and again, till the bore rose up and went off.

items.n: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting:13
items.e: Is it not writ in the 8th and 9th chapters of Medical Lore, that, as the quaternary fever is the visit of the heavy and dull?

items.n: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting:14
items.e: When a dull man visiteth thee at one time or another, and, stupidly chatting on a host of things, repeateth himself in his talk, then make thyself deaf, and pretend to be blind, act as though thou hast lost the use of thy feet, and as though thy mouth, in rebellion, had resolved not to speak.

items.n: On Visiting Friends and the Sick, and on Nuisances in Visiting:15
items.e: Visit a friend, visit the sick; but, pray, cease thou from visiting at all, if thou must needs be heavy and dull.

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:1
items.e: Before the tyrant or ruler shed not thy tears, for not alone will he mock thee, but he will also despise thee; so to the man without troubles reveal not thy sorrow, askance he'll look at thee, or he may not even regard thee.
items.h: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:2
items.e: Be ready to seek advice from all, whether they be young or old; at times thou mightest think it well to act on advice that cometh from a boor.

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:3
items.e: Reside in the place where thy fathers have dwelt, and set up thy dwelling in their old habitation; there's a place in the world for all who would dwell in it; e'en the bird nestles best in its own favourite nest.

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:4
items.e: To a woman a secret thou shouldst never disclose, lest for thy pains it bring thee derision; if thou dost prize dearly the life that is thine, quaff not the poison,—it's too great a trial.

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:5
items.e: He who entrusteth his possessions to his child or to his wife, will sure come to beggary, having first come to shame.

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:6
items.e: He that chideth him who refuseth to take sound advice, who speaketh to hearts that are closed, is like one who singeth a song to the dead, or crieth in prayer to the shades.

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:7
items.e: The man of sense needs but few words whereby he may profit, and be corrected; understanding well, he will see the purpose of things; he will fix them deep within his heart, and grasp them from end to end.

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:8
items.e: The man always laughing is a fool, and for his folly there is no cure and relief; at the time when he showeth his teeth, he loseth his dignity and honour.

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:9
items.e: Take a long time to make up thy mind, and then shall thy actions be perfectly sound; for the garden-fruit that is late in appearing will always be sweeter and far more mature.

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:10
items.e: Spend not thy strength, O wise one, in the attempt to overcome the wicked; but being strong and all-daring, oppose a bold front; for oft in his net the victor will fall, and the conquered will truly the conqueror be named.

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:11
items.e: In speaking, a stupid man will send his tongue in advance of his good sense; but a man of sense will check his tongue, and let prudence keep it back.

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:12
items.e: The fool in mischief findeth his sport; hence his reason cometh after his tongue; but the man of sense delayeth his words, and beginneth no matter until he hath grasped it.

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:13
items.e: He who promiseth a gift from day to day, sickeneth the heart with hope deferred; as the lowering clouds, that rainless pass, cover the face of the earth with gloom.

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:14
items.e: If thy soul shall fulness have, and poverty thou dost fear, then turn about, and take advice, and show thyself truly wise: of food take less, and duly shun the vice of gluttony; how little meat for proper folk will readily suffice! Too many wives, in the next place, see that thou dost avoid, and be on thy guard, lest thou dost sin, and thy strength unto strangers give. Whene'er thy soul desireth some object to attain, think, is not the price thou pay'st for it much too high and dear? Surely it is better by far to leave of thy riches to thy foes, than, recklessly spending all that thou hast, to beg cold charity of the wealthy.

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:15
items.e: When kindly fortune waiteth on man, the very stones on the road shall yield him bdellium and gold; and if it be destined that he shall succeed, the branch that is dry shall blossom in his hand; be assured and believe that on the day he doth sow, beautiful branches will bud and spring forth.

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:16
items.e: If thou listen to counsel, thou'lt shine forth bright, and thy soul shall be at ease with herself, finding favour with all.

items.n: Last Chapter of the Book; Collection of Maxims:17
items.e: ** Finished with the help of God. Blessed be He who giveth power to the weary, and to him who hath no strength He increaseth strength. **
